title: Battle Royale: Five AI Teacher Tools Try to Make the Same Worksheet
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer starts from Gallup's finding that 41 percent of K-12 teachers used no AI at all last year, and asks why reality lags so far behind the predictions of edtech boosters. He tests the question by asking Magic School, Brisk, Diffit and frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI to recreate a fifth-grade mixed-number subtraction worksheet, then asks people on social media which output they would assign. The reasons they give are about layout and typesetting details such as slanted fractions and missing work space, and an attempt to fix one tool's output made the fractions run off the printable page. His hypothesis is that most teachers prefer a predictable B-minus to a probabilistic A-plus, because the fiddly prompt-and-revise loop that technologists enjoy is stressful for overworked teachers. The post ends with featured comments and notes on studies of AI tutors and chatbots that found negligible or negative effects.
points: Gallup's survey shows 41 percent of teachers used no AI at all, a sharp gap with predictions that every educator would use it weekly.
Five AI tools given the same prompt produced worksheets with different but real flaws in layout and math typesetting, and revising them was unreliable.
Meyer's hypothesis is that teachers value predictable materials over high-variance ones that demand fiddling.
The same iteration loop that feels like a slot machine to technologists feels like added stress to teachers with a class starting in an hour.
The odds-and-ends section cites studies in which AI tutors and chatbots added little beyond videos and hints, or lowered grades.
quotes: Four years out from the release of ChatGPT, why is there such a mismatch between the expectations of technologists and the reality of teacher needs?
I hope we’d all agree that teachers shouldn’t have to do this kind of supplementary work.

Why does generative AI still lack the teacher usage enjoyed by email software, attendance software, digital projectors, or document cameras—technologies that have been in heavy use in 100% of the classes I visited in the 25-26 school year.
My hypothesis: most teachers would prefer materials that are a predictable B- to a probabilistic A+.
I don’t think many teachers have the time or inclination to fiddle—to translate a handout from their imagination into words and then fiddle with whatever an LLM produces from those words.
Fiddling is fun for a lot of people. You enter a slightly different prompt and get a result that is slightly closer to what you want.
For teachers—overworked and underresourced; class starting in an hour—I suspect that generative AI’s fiddly nature releases more cortisol than dopamine, more stress than relief.
Students want these conversations with their teachers. We’ve always been there to help students wrestle with the big issues, and this is a very big one.
